newsitem.title: USA: Dollar gains on Rubin comments.
newsitem.headline: Dollar gains on Rubin comments.

text.p: The dollar rose against the German mark Tuesday, bolstered by positive comments from U.S. officials and a strong showing by domestic stock and bond markets.
The dollar had sold off overnight along with the Treasury bond market as traders anticipated damaging remarks by Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan.
But Greenspan's speech to a Senate committee proved largely neutral, and the market focused on supportive comments from Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin.
Rubin told reporters in Washington he was not concerned that the strong dollar would hurt American exporters, helping the dollar rise against the mark, but not the Japanese yen.

"The comment from Rubin specifically saying he wasn't concerned about the strong dollar's effect on the U.S. trade deficit obviously should have had more influence on (the dollar against the yen)," said Stephen Flanagan, vice president at Credit Agricole.
New York Federal Reserve Bank President William McDonough echoed Rubin's consistent support for a strong dollar.

The dollar ended higher at 1.6296 marks vs. 1.6252 at Monday's close, but edged lower to 117.91 Japanese yen from 118.05. The dollar also rose to 1.4180 Swiss francs from 1.4165. The British pound was at $1.6635 vs. $1.6625.
The dollar had slipped against the yen early in the session after comments from Japanese Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka, who called the yen's recent slide "excessive" and "undesirable."
But investors have heard many such comments recently, and traders said Japanese officials would have to intervene directly in the market to buy yen to have a lasting impact on currency rates.

"You are going to run into some comments, but overall the trend is still higher," said James Powers, vice president at Westdeutsche Landesbank Girozentrale. "In the long run, these comments won't have much (impact) unless you back it up with something."

The dollar failed to hold above 118 yen after reaching a nearly four-year high Monday. Traders said many investors were reluctant to buy the dollar after its sharp recent gains have boosted its market value.
"Everybody is very sceptical about buying at these high levels, especially against the yen, said Flanagan.
The dollar got a lift from U.S. markets, which rallied after Greenspan's comments. The Dow Jones industrials rose 40.03 points to 6,883.90, a record high.
Greenspan warned of the risks of wage-driven inflation in the future, but his upbeat assesment of the U.S. economy helped bolster stocks and the dollar.

The market was especially sensitive to Greenspan's comments after the Fed chief spoke in early December about "irrational exuberance" in financial markets, which jolted stocks, bonds and the dollar at the time.

The markets "had an early sell-off in anticipaton of (the statement by) Greenspan," said John Barlow, senior dealer at Bayerische Landesbank Girozentrale. "He didn't say anything too exciting except that the economy is rolling along and that should continue to underpin the dollar."
